newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir leader says no firm word on hostages.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir leader says no firm word on hostages.

text.p: The chief minister of India's Jammu and Kashmir state said on Monday that authorities had not confirmed a captured militant's claim that four Westerners kidnapped two years ago had been shot dead.
"There is no complete and concrete information about the hostages so far," Farooq Abdullah told reporters in the state's summer capital, Srinagar.
"The recent press reports about the killing of hostages are all conjectures."

A pro-government militiaman and a Kashmiri newspaper said on Saturday that Nazir Ahmad Najar of the Harkat-ul-Ansar group told authorities that the four tourists had been shot in early 1996 and buried in a cave.
Najar told authorities of the murders after he was arrested last month in a joint operation involving police and a pro-government militia group called J.K. Ikhwan.
Britons Paul Wells and Keith Mangan, American Donald Hutchings and German Dirk Hasert were abducted while trekking in the Himalayan region in July 1995 by a previously unknown group, Al-Faran.
Al-Faran beheaded a fifth hostage, Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe, in August 1995.

Najar, also known as Nazir Chhaan, said the four hostages were killed in the Magam forest near Kokernag town, some 85 km (55 miles) south of Srinagar in January 1996, six months after they were captured.
Najar's account closely resembled a statement made last year by another captured militant, Nazir Mohammad, who also said the hostages had been killed in the Magam forest.
"We have a man in custody, his stories are all false," Abdullah said without identifying the man. "We combined all that information he has given, there is nothing. We have not succeeded there."
Negotiations between Indian authorities and the abductors broke off in late 1995, and officials and diplomats say they have no firm evidence to indicate whether the hostages are dead or alive.
Indian authorities and the hostages' relatives have said Al-Faran was backed by the Pakistan-based Harkat-ul-Ansar, which denies any links to Al-Faran.
